scope: AI scientist and automated machine-learning research systems
LLM-guided hypothesis generation linked to executable experiments
Agentic experimentation in computational science, simulation, and laboratory settings
Multi-agent research workflows with critic, evaluator, or self-improvement loops
Benchmarks and evaluations of autonomous research capability
exclusions: Generic LLM agent frameworks without a research-specific closed loop.
Papers limited to literature review, retrieval, summarization, or scientific question answering.
Hypothesis-generation-only systems that do not test or evaluate hypotheses.
Experiment-planning systems that do not execute experiments or consume resulting observations.
Opinion pieces, position papers, marketing pages, and unsupported project descriptions.
Autonomous coding agents unless their explicit objective is scientific or machine-learning research and they evaluate iterative research outcomes.
constraints: Prioritize papers that describe an end-to-end or substantially closed research loop: hypothesis generation, experiment design or execution, result evaluation, and iterative refinement.
Include systems using executable computational experiments, simulations, code, laboratory automation, or structured tool use.
Capture system architecture, degree of autonomy, human involvement, research domain, evaluation methodology, iteration mechanism, artifacts produced, and reported limitations.
Prefer primary papers with concrete system evaluations, ablations, case studies, or reproducible artifacts.
Include influential foundational work plus recent work available through September 21, 2026.

screeningCriteria: The paper presents or rigorously evaluates a research-oriented system using one or more LLM agents.
The system covers at least three stages of the loop, with strong preference for all four: hypothesis generation, experiment execution, result evaluation, and iterative refinement.
Experiment execution is operational rather than merely proposed: code, simulation, tools, instruments, or another environment produces observations.
The paper provides evidence sufficient to assess autonomy and effectiveness, such as task success, novelty, correctness, reproducibility, human intervention, cost, failure modes, or expert review.
The work adds a distinct architecture, domain, evaluation method, or empirical finding rather than duplicating another recommendation.

createdFrom.reference: User request on September 21, 2026: papers on autonomous research using LLMs, focused on agents that generate hypotheses, run experiments, evaluate results, and iteratively improve research.
